statement:
Explain why the use of the substitution $x=\dfrac1t$ does not demonstrate that the integrals
$$\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx \quad \text{and} \quad \int_{-1}^{1}\frac{-t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}\,dt$$
are equal.

Evaluate both integrals correctly.
solution:
**Why the substitution fails.** The substitution $x=1/t$ is not defined at $x=0$, but $0$ lies in the interval $[-1,1]$. A change of variable requires the substitution to be one-to-one and differentiable on the whole interval of integration; here it is not, so the naive substitution is invalid. (One would need to split at $0$ and treat each half as an improper integral.)

**First integral.** By symmetry,
$$\int_{-1}^1\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx=2\int_0^1\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2}\,dx.$$
Substituting $x=\tan\theta$ (so $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $1+x^2=\sec^2\theta$):
$$2\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\sec^2\theta}{\sec^4\theta}\,d\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta=\left[\theta+\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/4}=\frac\pi4+\frac12.$$

**Second integral.**
$$\int_{-1}^1\frac{-t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}\,dt=-2\int_0^1\frac{t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}\,dt.$$
Using $\dfrac{t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}=\dfrac{1}{1+t^2}-\dfrac{1}{(1+t^2)^2}$, we have
$$-2\int_0^1\left(\frac{1}{1+t^2}-\frac{1}{(1+t^2)^2}\right)dt=-2\left(\left[\tan^{-1}t\right]_0^1-\int_0^1\frac{1}{(1+t^2)^2}dt\right).$$
Using the first result $\int_0^1\frac{1}{(1+t^2)^2}dt=\tfrac12(\tfrac\pi4+\tfrac12)=\tfrac\pi8+\tfrac14$,
$$-2\left(\frac\pi4-\frac\pi8-\frac14\right)=-2\left(\frac\pi8-\frac14\right)=\frac12-\frac\pi4.$$

The two integrals are $\dfrac12+\dfrac\pi4$ and $\dfrac12-\dfrac\pi4$, which are not equal.
hints: The substitution x=1/t is undefined at x=0, which lies in the interval.
Use x=tan θ for the first integral (it is even).
